subtopic_detail: Postprandial vomiting of recognisable food with erratic glucose readings in long standing type 1 diabetes and a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 38 year old woman with type 1 diabetes of twenty two years who has four months of fullness after a few mouthfuls, nausea and vomiting of recognisable food several hours after eating.

Her continuous glucose monitor shows lows two hours after her meal boluses and highs four to six hours later, and she has stopped bolusing before meals because of the lows. She takes no opioid or anticholinergic medicine and has never used a glucagon like peptide 1 agonist. Her most recent haemoglobin A1c was 9.4 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop in blood pressure
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, abdomen soft with a succussion splash and no organomegaly or mass, absent ankle reflexes with reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, background diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy reporting retained food in the stomach with no ulcer, stricture or outlet obstruction, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, haemoglobin A1c 9.4 per cent (target under 7.0 per cent), urine albumin creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol (less than 2.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast to exclude a mechanical cause for her symptoms
options.rationale: Mechanical obstruction has already been excluded at endoscopy, which visualised the pylorus and duodenum directly and found retained food without a stricture. Cross sectional imaging is reserved for cases where endoscopy is incomplete or an extrinsic compressing lesion is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: A twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH study performed after her acid suppressing therapy has been withheld
options.rationale: Reflux monitoring addresses heartburn and regurgitation of acid rather than vomiting of recognisable food hours after a meal with a succussion splash. It measures oesophageal acid exposure and says nothing about gastric emptying. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: Antroduodenal manometry to characterise the contractile pattern of the gastric antrum and the proximal small bowel
options.rationale: Antroduodenal manometry is a specialised test used in tertiary centres to investigate suspected generalised intestinal dysmotility when simpler tests are unhelpful. It is not the initial test for suspected delayed gastric emptying. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: A urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori with repeat gastroscopy and antral biopsies if the breath test is positive
options.rationale: Helicobacter pylori causes ulcer disease and dyspepsia rather than retained food with a succussion splash, and her endoscopy showed no ulceration. Eradication would not alter symptoms driven by impaired gastric motor function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: Solid phase gastric emptying scintigraphy performed over four hours with her glucose in the target range on the day
options.rationale: Four hour solid phase scintigraphy is the reference standard for delayed gastric emptying and is the test that converts a clinical suspicion into a diagnosis that justifies prokinetic therapy and insulin timing changes. Acute hyperglycaemia itself slows emptying, so the study is performed with glucose reasonably controlled to avoid a falsely abnormal result. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes complications position statement)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes complications position statement

explanation.summary: Diabetic gastroparesis is a manifestation of autonomic neuropathy that typically appears after many years of diabetes and is usually accompanied by other evidence of neuropathy such as absent ankle reflexes, retinopathy or albuminuria. The characteristic story is early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting of food eaten hours earlier, together with the distinctive glycaemic signature of hypoglycaemia soon after a meal bolus followed by later hyperglycaemia as delayed absorption occurs. Endoscopy is done first to exclude mechanical obstruction and ulceration, and four hour solid phase scintigraphy then confirms delayed emptying, performed with glucose reasonably controlled because acute hyperglycaemia slows emptying in its own right and drugs including opioids, anticholinergics and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists must be withheld beforehand. Management combines small frequent low fat low fibre meals, optimisation of glycaemic control, a short course of a prokinetic such as metoclopramide with attention to its extrapyramidal risk on prolonged use, antiemetics, and adjustment of insulin timing to match delayed absorption. Refractory cases are referred for consideration of enteral feeding beyond the stomach or specialist interventions.
key_points: Gastroparesis usually occurs with other evidence of autonomic and peripheral neuropathy after long standing diabetes.
Postprandial hypoglycaemia followed by later hyperglycaemia is a characteristic glycaemic pattern.
Endoscopy first excludes mechanical obstruction; scintigraphy then confirms delayed emptying.
Acute hyperglycaemia and drugs such as opioids and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists slow emptying and must be accounted for before testing.
Treatment combines dietary modification, glycaemic optimisation, prokinetics and insulin timing adjustment.
explanation.pearls: Metoclopramide carries a cumulative risk of tardive dyskinesia and Australian practice limits it to short courses, so a prokinetic is prescribed for defined periods with review rather than added to a repeat prescription indefinitely.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes complications position statement

subtopic_detail: A shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus with oedema and pigmentation in a woman with palpable foot pulses
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old woman with a shallow ulcer above the inner ankle that has been present for ten weeks. It weeps clear fluid, aches at the end of the day and eases when she puts her legs up.

She has hypertension and a body mass index of 34 kg/m2, and she had a deep vein thrombosis in that leg after a knee replacement twelve years ago. A practice nurse has been dressing it weekly with a foam dressing and has asked you whether antibiotics are needed.

data_table.Examination: Shallow ulcer of 4 cm by 3 cm above the medial malleolus with a flat granulating base and irregular sloping edges, surrounding brown pigmentation with induration of the gaiter area, pitting oedema to the mid calf, varicose veins in the great saphenous distribution, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable bilaterally, normal sensation to monofilament testing, no surrounding warmth beyond the ulcer margin and no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin A1c 5.4 per cent (under 6.0 per cent), full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), wound swab growing mixed skin flora

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for seven days on the basis of the mixed growth from her wound swab
options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised, and mixed skin flora on a swab from a wound without spreading erythema, increasing pain, purulence or systemic features does not indicate infection. Antibiotics for colonisation drive resistance without accelerating healing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Prescribe pentoxifylline and continue the current weekly dressing regimen with review of the ulcer in six weeks
options.rationale: Pentoxifylline has modest evidence as an adjunct to compression but no role as a substitute for it, and continuing dressings alone leaves the venous hypertension that is causing the ulcer untreated. Adjuncts are considered once compression is established. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Refer her for a split skin graft to the ulcer bed and arrange the procedure through the plastic surgery service
options.rationale: Grafting is considered for large or refractory ulcers after compression has failed, and a graft applied without correcting venous hypertension will break down. Definitive treatment of the underlying haemodynamic problem comes first. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Measure the ankle brachial pressure index and commence graduated multilayer compression bandaging
options.rationale: Compression is the intervention that heals venous ulcers, roughly doubling healing rates compared with dressings alone, and the ankle brachial pressure index is measured first because significant arterial disease makes full compression unsafe. Palpable pulses are reassuring but are not a substitute for the measurement in an older patient with cardiovascular risk factors. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Arrange a punch biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude malignancy before any compression therapy is commenced
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for an ulcer with rolled or everted edges, atypical appearance or failure to heal despite three months of adequate compression, because squamous cell carcinoma can arise in chronic ulcers. A typical venous ulcer that has not yet had compression does not warrant biopsy first. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

explanation.summary: Venous leg ulcers account for the large majority of chronic lower limb ulcers and arise from sustained venous hypertension, often after deep vein thrombosis or with superficial venous incompetence and obesity. The typical ulcer sits in the gaiter area, most often above the medial malleolus, is shallow with sloping edges and a granulating base, and is surrounded by haemosiderin pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis and oedema, with pain relieved by elevation. Graduated multilayer compression is the treatment that heals them, and an ankle brachial pressure index is measured beforehand because compression is unsafe in significant arterial disease, with an index below about 0.8 prompting modified compression or vascular referral and an index below 0.5 contraindicating it. Wound swabs are not taken routinely because all chronic ulcers are colonised, and antibiotics are reserved for clinical infection with spreading erythema, increasing pain, purulence or systemic features. Adjuncts include leg elevation, exercise of the calf pump, weight management, pentoxifylline, and referral for assessment of superficial venous incompetence, which reduces recurrence, and ulcers failing to heal after three months of adequate compression are biopsied to exclude malignancy.
key_points: Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area with pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis and oedema, and ease with elevation.
Graduated compression is the definitive treatment and roughly doubles healing rates compared with dressings alone.
An ankle brachial pressure index is measured before compression because arterial disease makes it unsafe.
Swabs grow colonising flora, and antibiotics are reserved for clinical signs of infection.
An ulcer that has not healed after three months of adequate compression is biopsied for malignancy.
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 is as concerning as a low one, because incompressible calcified vessels in diabetes and chronic kidney disease produce a falsely high reading, and in that situation toe pressures or a waveform assessment are used before compression is applied.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers
BMJ Best Practice: Venous leg ulcer

subtopic_detail: Macrocytic anaemia with neutropenia and dysplastic changes on the film in an older man with normal vitamin levels
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 78 year old man referred with four months of increasing breathlessness on walking to his letterbox. He has had two courses of antibiotics for chest infections this winter.

He drinks two beers on a Friday, takes perindopril and atorvastatin, and has had no melaena, rectal bleeding or weight loss. His colonoscopy two years ago for bowel screening was normal apart from two small hyperplastic polyps.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or petechiae, no glossitis, chest clear on auscultation, neurological examination with normal vibration and proprioception and normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 84 g/L (130 to 180), mean cell volume 106 fL (80 to 100), white cell count 3.1 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L, platelets 92 x10^9/L (150 to 400), reticulocytes 22 x10^9/L (20 to 100), blood film showing hypogranular neutrophils with bilobed nuclei and occasional macro-ovalocytes with no blasts, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, ferritin 210 micrograms/L (30 to 300), direct antiglobulin test negative, erythropoietin 180 IU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and oral folate, and repeat the full blood count in six weeks
options.rationale: Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin deficiency is excluded by normal B12 and folate levels with normal neurological examination, and empirical replacement would simply delay diagnosis. Hypersegmented neutrophils rather than hypogranular bilobed forms would be the film finding in deficiency. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

options.text: Arrange upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy to identify a source of occult blood loss causing his anaemia
options.rationale: Endoscopy is the pathway for iron deficiency anaemia, which is microcytic with a low ferritin and low transferrin saturation, whereas his indices are macrocytic with a normal ferritin. The neutropenia and thrombocytopenia also point to a production problem rather than to blood loss. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells and arrange a repeat full blood count with clinical review in three months
options.rationale: Transfusion relieves symptoms and will be part of his supportive care, but it does not explain a trilineage abnormality with a dysplastic film, and three months of transfusion alone allows iron loading and leaves the diagnosis unmade. Transfusion accompanies the diagnostic pathway rather than replacing it. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and perindopril as likely causes of his cytopenias, and recheck his blood count in one month
options.rationale: Drug induced cytopenias are worth considering, but neither of these agents typically produces macrocytosis with dysplastic morphology across three lineages. Stopping them delays a diagnosis that a marrow examination would establish now. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Refer him for bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic and molecular studies through haematology
options.rationale: Macrocytic anaemia with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, dysplastic neutrophils on the film and normal vitamin levels describe a marrow production disorder, and bone marrow examination with cytogenetics and molecular testing is what confirms myelodysplastic syndrome and assigns the risk group. Risk stratification determines whether he receives supportive care, erythropoiesis stimulating therapy or a hypomethylating agent. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

explanation.summary: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal disorders of haematopoietic stem cells that mainly affect people over seventy and present with cytopenias arising from ineffective haematopoiesis, most often a macrocytic or normocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte response, sometimes accompanied by neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The blood film provides the first clue, showing dysplastic features such as hypogranular neutrophils, the bilobed pseudo Pelger Huet form, macro-ovalocytes and giant or hypogranular platelets. Reversible causes are excluded first, including vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, alcohol, thyroid disease, liver disease, haemolysis, copper deficiency and drugs, and the diagnosis is then confirmed with bone marrow aspirate and trephine including cytogenetics and molecular studies. Risk stratification using the revised international prognostic scoring system drives management, which ranges from transfusion support and erythropoiesis stimulating agents in lower risk disease to hypomethylating agents and, in fit younger patients, allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Progression to acute myeloid leukaemia occurs in a minority, and iron chelation is considered for transfusion dependent patients with a reasonable life expectancy.
key_points: Unexplained cytopenias in an older person with a macrocytic anaemia and a low reticulocyte count suggest marrow failure.
Hypogranular neutrophils with bilobed nuclei on the film are strongly suggestive of dysplasia.
Reversible causes including vitamin deficiency, alcohol, thyroid and liver disease and drugs are excluded first.
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics confirms the diagnosis and enables risk stratification.
Management ranges from supportive care in lower risk disease to hypomethylating agents or transplantation in higher risk disease.
explanation.pearls: A serum erythropoietin level below about 500 IU/L in lower risk disease predicts a worthwhile response to an erythropoiesis stimulating agent, which is why it is measured before transfusion rather than after, since transfusion suppresses the endogenous level and makes the result uninterpretable.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myelodysplastic syndromes position statement

subtopic_detail: An incidental sustained lymphocytosis of twenty two in a well man with no lymphadenopathy or cytopenias
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 67 year old man whose blood count was taken as part of a preoperative check before a cataract operation. He feels entirely well, plays golf twice a week and has lost no weight.

He has had no fevers, drenching night sweats or unusual infections. A count taken eight weeks ago showed a lymphocyte count of 19 x10^9/L, and today's shows 22 x10^9/L. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and no other medical history.

data_table.Examination: No cervical, axillary or inguinal lymphadenopathy, no hepatomegaly, spleen not palpable, no pallor, no bruising or petechiae, no skin lesions, tonsils not enlarged
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130 to 180), white cell count 26.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with lymphocytes 22.1 x10^9/L and neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L, platelets 212 x10^9/L (150 to 400), blood film showing small mature lymphocytes with scattered smudge cells and no blasts, lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Peripheral blood flow cytometry to immunophenotype the circulating lymphocytes and confirm clonality
options.rationale: A sustained monoclonal lymphocytosis with small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells is diagnosed by immunophenotyping on peripheral blood, which demonstrates the characteristic surface marker pattern and light chain restriction without any need for tissue sampling. Establishing the diagnosis this way avoids an invasive procedure in a man who is otherwise well. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Excisional lymph node biopsy of an accessible node with histology and immunohistochemistry to classify the lymphoid disorder
options.rationale: Node biopsy is the procedure for a lymphadenopathic presentation or where transformation to a high grade lymphoma is suspected, signalled by rapid node growth, systemic symptoms and a rising lactate dehydrogenase. He has no palpable nodes to sample. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with cytogenetic studies to assess the degree of marrow infiltration present
options.rationale: Marrow examination is not required for diagnosis when the peripheral blood immunophenotype is characteristic, and it is reserved for unexplained cytopenias or for assessing an unclear response to treatment. Performing it first adds risk and discomfort without adding information. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Computed tomography of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast to stage the extent of nodal involvement
options.rationale: Routine staging imaging is not recommended for an asymptomatic patient in whom treatment is not being contemplated, because it does not change management and delivers radiation. Imaging is used at the point of treatment decisions or when bulky disease or transformation is suspected. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

options.text: Repeat the full blood count with a film in twelve months and refer him only if the lymphocyte count has risen further
options.rationale: Simple observation without characterisation cannot distinguish this from mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase or another lymphoproliferative disorder with a very different prognosis and treatment. Watchful waiting is appropriate after the diagnosis is established, not instead of establishing it. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement

explanation.summary: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the commonest leukaemia in Australian adults and is increasingly found incidentally on a blood count taken for another reason, in a person who feels entirely well. The diagnosis requires a monoclonal B lymphocyte count of at least 5 x10 to the power of 9 per litre in the peripheral blood with a characteristic immunophenotype, and peripheral blood flow cytometry is therefore the diagnostic test, making marrow examination and node biopsy unnecessary in a typical case. The important mimic is mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase, which shares a mature B cell appearance but has a markedly worse prognosis and is separated by immunophenotype and cyclin D1 or translocation testing. Most patients with early stage disease need no treatment, and observation with periodic clinical review and blood counts is the standard, with treatment triggered by progressive marrow failure, bulky or symptomatic lymphadenopathy, massive splenomegaly, rapid lymphocyte doubling or constitutional symptoms. Complications include hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent infection, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia, and transformation to high grade lymphoma, so vaccination and infection awareness are part of long term care.
key_points: Peripheral blood flow cytometry establishes the diagnosis without marrow or node sampling in typical cases.
Smudge cells with small mature lymphocytes on the film are characteristic but not by themselves diagnostic.
Mantle cell lymphoma in leukaemic phase is the key mimic and is separated by immunophenotype.
Routine staging imaging is not recommended when treatment is not being contemplated.
Treatment is triggered by marrow failure, symptomatic bulk, rapid doubling or constitutional symptoms, not by the count alone.
explanation.pearls: A lymphocyte doubling time of less than twelve months is one of the recognised triggers for treatment, which is why the date and value of every previous blood count matter more than any single result at referral.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia position statement
